Pilot 3 Readout

First field of the full 132-question instrument: typed alternative on the mic gate, bundled take-all network wall and sports wall, EV / solar / plant-based modules. A living readout — the field was open at generation time.

01

Overview

Pilot 3 is the first field of the full Wave-2 instrument: 132 questions on 71 pages, published to the Forthright/Bovitz link on Sep 11 (3:52 PM ET, source 97984e59, survey-engine 2.9.1). Three design changes since pilot 2 are visible in the numbers: a first-class typed alternative on the spoken bot check (ADR 0051), the bundled take-all network wall plus a nine-card sports wall (ADR 0052/0053), and the EV, solar and plant-based behavior modules. Bovitz released traffic on Saturday Sep 12 and again Sunday Sep 13; data below run through Sep 13, 2026 5:57 PM ET and the field was still open at generation time.

The pilot in one paragraph. The typed alternative did what it was designed to do: landing losses fell from 37% of arrivals in pilot 2 to 12% here, and 168 of the 405 entrants (41%) came in by keyboard. The price is a longer survey: median active time rose from 15.5 to 21.9 minutes (132 vs 79 questions), and mid-survey abandonment edged up — 73 entrants (18% of landing-clearers) parked somewhere inside the survey versus 16% in pilot 2, a third of them on the two show walls. Completion among landing-clearers still ran 73%, and overall yield per arrival (65%) is the best of the three pilots. Voice uptake on the open items fell from 52% to 41% of answers, and the gate route explains all of it: entrants who typed the phrase almost never used the microphone afterwards (3% of their 277 open answers), while those who spoke it used voice for 67% of theirs (58% among pilot 2’s spoken passers).

Two afternoon releases, Saturday and Sunday, each converting within the hour. Times are Eastern.

03

The landing gate, with a keyboard

The landing keeps the microphone as the primary ask (“Voice verification is the only reliable way to keep bots out”) and adds a “Type instead” link (ADR 0051). Turnstile is gone from this landing; the honeypot remains. Every arrival is still probed and every tap logged, so each of the 53 landing losses has a cause.

gate outcomes

Four ways off the landing page

Every arrival ends the landing in one of these states.

mic gatebase: all 458 arrivals

Landing losses fell to 12% of arrivals (37% in pilot 2, 60% in pilot 1). The refusal-to-engage loss that dominated the first two pilots — read the ask, leave without a tap — is down to 37 arrivals (8%; 25% in pilot 2), most of them on desktop (23 of 37). 16 tried the mic and left without typing.

typed route

168 entrants typed the phrase — 99 cold, 69 after a microphone try

Typed entries by whether the participant had already tapped or recorded.

ADR 0051base: 168 typed entrants

Two populations use the keyboard. 99 entrants (24% of all landing-clearers) opened “Type instead” without ever tapping the microphone — these are people pilot 2 would have lost as never-tapped, or would never have counted at all. The other 69 reached the keyboard through a recovery panel after a real failure: 41 panels for a microphone the browser could not open, 30 for an unanswered permission prompt, 11 for a denied one, 8 for a timed-out request. Typed entrants carry Botcheck_Voice.Passed = 0 by design; bot-rate analyses must condition on Botcheck_Voice.Fallback.

spoken route

220 of 237 spoken passes came on the first attempt

Spoken attempts logged in _botcheck_voice_attempts.

telemetrybase: 237 spoken passers

Across all arrivals the log holds 421 attempt records: 226 passes, 12 phrase mismatches, 13 transcription failures, 7 silent recordings and 163 blocked taps. The gate’s audio is retained: 273 gate utterances from 250 arrivals, mean 4.2s.

capability probe

What arrivals brought to the page

Passive probe at page load: permission state, input devices, secure context.

telemetrybase: 458 probed arrivals

97% of arrivals had never been asked for their microphone. 27 arrivals reported no microphone at all — in pilot 2 these were automatic gate deaths; here the keyboard is available to them from the first screen.

friction

71 arrivals fought a blocked microphone

attempt_mic_blocked records and on-page notices at the gate.

telemetrybase: 71 arrivals with a blocked tap

Permission friction is unchanged in kind from pilot 2 — 73 arrivals hit a not-granted state at least once (51 phones, 19 desktops) and 38 retried the mic — but it no longer ends the session: nearly all of it now drains into the typed route (section above). Transcription failures at the gate dropped to 14 notices.

Reloading the landing page resets the in-memory event log, so per-arrival struggle counts are lower bounds.

gate variables

Gate outcome variables as stored

Distribution of the bot-check response keys over completes.

data contractbase: 297 completes

Every complete carries Passed and Used; Fallback exists only for typed entrants. 2 completes still carry a Turnstile key — resumed sessions whose stored state predates the Sep-11 build — and the honeypot was never touched. Botcheck_Voice.Confirmation itself is ephemeral and never written.

04

Drop-off: where the non-completes stand

161 arrivals had not completed at generation time: 53 lost on the landing, 35 terminated by the attention row, and 73 parked or abandoned somewhere inside the 71-page survey. This is the first pilot where the inside-the-survey loss is larger than the landing loss.

non-completes

Three kinds of loss, 161 entrants

Non-completes by where they stopped.

drop-offbase: all 458 arrivals

Landing loss: 12% of arrivals (pilot 2: 37%; pilot 1: 60%). Mid-survey abandonment: 18% of landing-clearers (pilot 2: 16%; pilot 1: 6%). Some of the 73 will still convert while the field is open — pilot 2’s parked rows converted for days — so read the mid-survey figure as an upper bound at this snapshot.

by section

drop-offbase: 405 landing-clearers

The show walls and streaming block account for 24 of 73 mid-survey losses (33%) — 10 at the practice round, 9 on the 59-card network wall, 2 on the streamer wall, 1 on the sports wall. The new EV / solar / plant-based modules lost 11 (3% of landing-clearers) spread thinly across their pages; media hours lost 8 at the consumption-hours page, the same page that led pilot 2’s mid-survey losses.

Non-completes parked on each page, with the page number in the 71-page order.

drop-offbase: 405 landing-clearers

No single page inside the survey loses more than 10 entrants (2% of clearers). The pattern is a slow leak concentrated early: 36 of the 73 mid-survey losses happen in the first 14 pages (media habits, walls, streaming, hours), 13 in the last 26 (the behavior modules, policy, demographics).

time by section

Where the minutes go — pilot 3 vs pilot 2

Sum of per-page median active seconds within each section, completes only.

timingbases: 297 vs 143 completes

Summing page medians gives 19.0 minutes for pilot 3 against 13.6 for pilot 2. The new EV / solar / plant-based modules add 3.5 minutes on their own; the show walls take 4.0 minutes (3.8 in pilot 2 — the bundled take-all network wall shows 59 cards to everyone where pilot 2 sampled). The network wall page alone medians 97s and the streamer wall 82s; every other page medians under a minute.

05

Three Bovitz pilots, compared

Same panel, same hub link, three landings and three instrument lengths. Pilot 1 (Aug 28–31): 74 questions, desktop-only gate, strict spoken check, no telemetry — 213 arrivals. Pilot 2 (Sep 1–3): 79 questions, phones admitted, strict spoken check with telemetry — 302 arrivals. Pilot 3 (Sep 12–13): 132 questions, typed alternative on the check — 458 arrivals. All three are recomputed here with one set of rules (team, localhost and pre-publish rows excluded; pilot 2 therefore reads 302/143 rather than the 318/145 on its own tab, which counted 16 team rows).

funnel

Share of arrivals reaching each state

Percent of arrivals, pilot by pilot.

comparisonbases: 213 · 302 · 458 arrivals

Landing clearance climbed 40% → 63% → 88%: admitting phones bought the first jump, the keyboard the second. Completion per arrival followed, 33% → 47% → 65%. The never-tapped refusal that was 56% of pilot 1 is 8% here. Attention terminations ran 4%, 6% and 8% of arrivals — a higher share in pilot 3 partly because more arrivals now reach the attention row at all.

conditional rates

Once past the landing

Rates among landing-clearers — the like-for-like view of survey length and content.

comparisonbases: 85 · 191 · 405 landing-clearers

This is the cost of the full instrument. Completion among clearers was 84% at 74 questions, 75% at 79, 73% at 132; mid-survey abandonment rose from 6% and 16% to 18%. Part of the pilot-3 figure is the open field (parked rows can still convert) and part is the keyboard admitting entrants who were less committed to begin with — but the length effect is real: the abandonment sits on the longest pages. Attention terminations among clearers are stable at 9–11%.

devices

Device mix and device outcomes

Arrival shares by device, and clearance/completion within phones and desktops.

comparisoncapability probe (p2, p3) / user agent (p1)

Pilot 1 saw only desktops (its device gate bounced everything else). Pilot 2’s natural mix was 49% phone; pilot 3’s weekend traffic was 60% phone. Desktop clearance is where the keyboard mattered most: 40% → 60% → 81%. Phones cleared at 65% in pilot 2 and 93% here.

time and voice

Length, time and voice uptake

Median active minutes per complete; voice share of open-ended answers.

comparison

Active time scales with the instrument: roughly 11s, 12s and 10s per question across the three pilots, so the extra minutes are content, not friction. Voice uptake fell from 52% to 41% of open answers, and the split by gate route accounts for the whole drop: spoken-gate entrants used voice for 67% of their answers, typed-gate entrants for 3%. The keyboard admits a population that does not want to speak — self-selection, not evidence that the spoken gate causes later voice use (the randomized Sep-3 Connect landing pilot found no such effect). For voice-dependent analyses, the voice-eligible base is the spoken-gate share of entrants, 59% here.

06

Voice, rotation and the open items

The five ungated voice probes still rotate two per participant; the similarity-gated who-cares probe rides on top for those at similarity 1–2 (99 of 297 completes, 33%). Every shown item was answered.

draw balance

Rotation draws stayed near the 40% expectation

Times each item was shown over completes with a draw record.

planned missingnessbase: 297 completes

Items drew 37–42% against 40% expected; all ten pairs occurred (22–38 times). Draws are recorded per row, so residual imbalance is weightable.

uptake

286 of 693 open answers came by voice

Voice share per shown item, pilot 2 against pilot 3.

voice vs typedbases: 334 · 693 answers

Voice share is flat across items (36–45%) but down from pilot 2 (52% → 41%); the next article shows the drop is entirely the typed-gate population. By device: phones 46% voice (53% in pilot 2), desktops 33% (52%). Desktops, where half the entrants typed the gate, fell furthest.

gate route

Typed-gate entrants used voice for 3% of open answers; spoken-gate entrants for 67%

Voice share of open answers by how the participant cleared the landing (completes only).

voice vs typedbases: 416 answers from 177 spoken-gate completes · 277 from 120 typed-gate completes

The gate route is close to a perfect predictor of downstream input mode. Participants who chose the keyboard at the gate kept it: 8 voice answers in 277. Participants who spoke the phrase used the microphone for 67% of their open answers — higher than pilot 2’s spoken passers (58%), consistent with the keyboard having pulled the reluctant speakers out of that group. This is self-selection, not a gate effect: the Sep-3 Connect landing experiment randomized the gate and found no uptake difference. The practical consequence is that the voice corpus scales with the spoken-gate share (59% of entrants here), not with completes.

answer length

Voice answers average 23 words; typed 10

Mean words per answer by input mode, per item.

qualitybase: 286 voice / 407 typed

The richness gap holds for the third time: spoken answers run 2.3× the length of typed ones. Roughly 11% of all open answers are one-word or non-answers (“no”, “idk”, “nothing”), concentrated on the two trust items.

07

Open-ended answers, thematically coded

All 693 open answers were read and coded against the per-item codebooks used for pilot 2, so shares are comparable across pilots (answers can carry several codes; codes new to pilot 3 are marked). Chips mark voice or typed exemplars.

trust-messengers-open · page 20 · trust-messengers-world

TV-world trust

Who are some TV figures or celebrities that you trust to talk about the world?

thematic codingbase: 120 answers54 voice / 66 typed

Shared codes, pilot 2 → pilot 3 (share of answers)

I don't trust any TV figure or celebrity to talk about the world. Not one. They're there for entertainment purposes only. That's it. I could care less what they have to say about anything else. voice
none really, but jon stewart and others like him seem to tell the truth more often than the politicians or even the news personalities. typed
I would say I trust Oprah and Kamala Harris because they are well-educated and well-experienced women of the world. voice
I like the actor in Matrix: Keanu Reeves. I see the truth and honesty on his face. typed

The modal answer is a flat refusal: 40 of 120 (33%) trust no TV figure or celebrity, usually because celebrities are entertainers with no special qualification or have their own motives, and another 7 (6%) are unsure or cannot think of anyone. Almost as many, 39 (32.5%), name entertainers, athletes or musicians (Keanu Reeves 5 mentions; Tom Hanks, Dwayne Johnson, Zendaya, Billie Eilish, Dolly Parton, De Niro, BTS, Mbappé), and 16 (13%) name comedians or late-night hosts, driven by Jon Stewart, the single most-named figure with 9 mentions (Trevor Noah, John Oliver, Kimmel and Fallon trail; eleven further names tie at 2). Neil deGrasse Tyson (4) and Bill Nye (3) are the only non-entertainers named repeatedly; politicians (Trump, Obama, Clinton, Biden, Harris, Huckabee) appear in 5 answers (4%), journalists (Anderson Cooper, Brit Hume, Ann Curry, Fareed Zakaria, 'news reporters') in 7 (6%), talk/online commentators (Oprah, The View, Andy Cohen, Charlie Kirk, Sam Seder and Hasan Piker) in 5 (4%), and one new code was added for religious figures and TV preachers (3). Against pilot 2 the no-one share is slightly lower (33% vs 37%), entertainers slightly higher (32.5% vs 28%), comedians roughly double (13% vs 7%), politicians halve (4% vs 8%), and garbled or unusable answers rise to 11% (13) from 7%, including two typed mode-switch artifacts ('Allow', 'I want to type') and three typed names that could not be identified. Voice answers (54 of 120) are garbled about twice as often as typed ones (8 of 54, 15%, vs 5 of 66, 8%) and five voice transcripts came through wholly or partly in Russian or Chinese, but the substantive split is similar across modes (voice 35% no-one and 30% entertainers; typed 32% and 35%), with voice answers more often volunteering a reason. Most-named public figures: Jon Stewart (9), Keanu Reeves (5), Neil deGrasse Tyson (4), Bill Nye (3), Trevor Noah (2), Tom Hanks (2), Dwayne Johnson (2), Barack Obama (2).

13 answers garbled or unusable.

trust-messengers-open · page 20 · trust-messengers-climate

Climate trust

Who are some people you trust to talk about climate change? They don't have to be TV figures or celebrities — anyone counts.

thematic codingbase: 126 answers56 voice / 70 typed

Shared codes, pilot 2 → pilot 3 (share of answers)

Mostly it's the scientists that I trust with climate change, because they're the ones that are studying it and understand it. voice
Some people I trust to talk about climate change would be my best friend or my partner, maybe also some close family members. voice
No one. This has become an industry rather than a cause typed
I don't know specific names but,I'd say fishermen & people who travel oceans. Island countries, older farmers,scientists that have accumulated the data for years. typed

The modal answer is the personal circle: 35 of 126 (28%) name family, friends, partners, coworkers or neighbors, and scientists or relevant experts come second at 27 (21%), almost always stated generically ('scientists', 'professors', 'people who study weather'); only 13 answers name any public figure, led by Greta Thunberg (3) and Neil deGrasse Tyson (2), with DiCaprio, Bill Gates, Jon Stewart, Biden, Bill Clinton, RFK Jr., McConaughey, Billie Eilish, Rosario Dawson and the pope at one each. Distrust is far more visible than in pilot 2: 25 answers (20%) trust nobody or say everyone has an agenda or the information conflicts, 4 (3%) deny climate change or call it a natural cycle, and 8 (6%) are unsure or do not engage with the topic, so 35 answers (28%) fall in the nobody, denial or don't-know groups. Two new codes were added: 'Politicians / government' (7, 6%: the government, Democrats, Republicans, local leaders, Biden, Bill Clinton and RFK Jr.) and 'Don't know / disengaged' (8); one answer trusts fishermen, island communities and older farmers as lived-experience witnesses, and two cite a pastor and church group or the pope. Compared with pilot 2, scientists fall from 41% to 21%, family/friends hold steady (27% vs 28%), nobody/skeptical rises from 6% to 20%, named celebrities (5% vs 6%) and Greta Thunberg (3 vs 2 mentions) are flat, and nobody named a specific weather forecaster (8% in pilot 2) although six answers cited meteorologists or weather experts generically and are counted under scientists; garbled answers are 12 (10%) vs 8%. Voice answers (56 of 126) are garbled four times as often as typed ones (9 of 56, 16%, vs 3 of 70, 4%), including Russian and Portuguese fragments and one respondent reading the question back, and lean more toward family and personal circle (32% vs 24%), while scientists (20% vs 23%) and nobody (18% vs 21%) are similar across modes. Most-named public figures: Greta Thunberg (3), Neil deGrasse Tyson (2), Leonardo DiCaprio (1), Bill Gates (1), Jon Stewart (1), Joe Biden (1), Bill Clinton (1), Robert F. Kennedy Jr. (1).

12 answers garbled or unusable.

climate-solution-recall · page 24 · climate-solution-recall-open

Solutions recalled, unaided

In your opinion, what are some of the most effective ways to address climate change? Please list as many as you can think of.

thematic codingbase: 113 answers50 voice / 63 typed

Shared codes, pilot 2 → pilot 3 (share of answers)

Conserve resources and try to use less of things. Always try to recycle or repurpose. typed
Some of the most effective ways for us to combat climate change is cut back on our CO2 emissions, use clean energy, stop drilling so much. voice
We need to stop the AI data centers. We need to try to figure out a way to cool the Earth. voice
Collective action through legislation. Hardening of coastlines, reducing emissions, shoring up agricultural alternatives. Looking to help other nations and peoples who will be especially devastated. typed

Individual behavior change (recycling, using less, a smaller footprint) is the modal theme at 32 of 113 (28%), unchanged from pilot 2 (17 of 58, 29%); non-answers are 25 (22% vs 19%), 8 of them unusable captures such as stray audio, single foreign words and a truncated fragment. System-level answers are more common than in pilot 2: energy transition 19 (17% vs 9%; fossil-fuel phase-out, solar, wind, EVs, and one desktop respondent who ranks nuclear first and adds carbon taxes, fusion research and aerosol geoengineering) and government policy/voting 17 (15% vs 9%; this bucket holds 5 answers about international cooperation or pressuring China, India and Russia, one call to remove the current president and one lament for recently disbanded climate programs), while corporate accountability fell to 5 (4% vs 12%), denial/hoax to 9 (8% vs 12%) and education/media to 9 (8% vs 10%). Two new codes were needed: a generic cut-emissions/pollution bucket (13, 12%) for answers naming no actor or mechanism, and a fatalist nothing-can-be-done/leave-it-to-God stance (5, 4%) that is distinct from denial. AI data centers are named by 3 respondents (3% vs 7% in pilot 2); other one-offs include population control, stopping development, atmospheric water collection and two weather-modification conspiracy answers. Voice answers (50 of 113) run longer and carry more codes each, but 15 of 50 (30%) are non-answers versus 10 of 63 typed (16%), and 7 of the 8 unusable answers are voice.

8 answers garbled or unusable.

climate-efficacy · page 32 · climate-hope-open

What gives hope

What gives you hope when you think about humanity's efforts to mitigate, adapt and resolve climate change?

thematic codingbase: 110 answers40 voice / 70 typed

Shared codes, pilot 2 → pilot 3 (share of answers)

Actually, not much right now because, um, nobody's doing anything. voice
We have been adapting and resolving and mitigating s- for... since the beginning of mankind, and we will continue to do that. Whatever's thrown our way, we will adapt and overcome. That's human nature. voice
Seeing people work together to use renewable energy, protect nature, reduce pollution and create new climate friendly technologies. typed
The weather is getting so bad that it will force communities to take it seriously. typed

Little or no hope is the modal theme at 27 of 110 (25%), up from 9 of 55 (16%) in pilot 2, while vague/don't-know answers fell to 17 (15% vs 20%), 5 of them junk (two stray Allow strings, a lone punctuation mark, a keyboard mash, a foreign-word fragment). Collective action (14, 13% vs 16%) and rising awareness/generations/platforms (14, 13% vs 13%) hold steady; clean-tech advances jumped to 13 (12% vs 4%), though 7 of those cite science or technology in general rather than clean tech specifically, and human resilience/adaptability doubled to 11 (10% vs 5%). Visible local action and greener products dropped to 6 (5% vs 13%), leaders/legislation is 7 (6% vs 5%; several make hope conditional on a change of administration, and one names the current president as the source of hope), and denial is 5 (5% vs 7%). Two new codes: crises will force action (7, 6%; worsening weather, disasters or the pandemic pause as catalysts) and faith in God (4, 4%). Voice answers (40 of 110) skew to no hope (13 of 40, 33% vs 14 of 70 typed, 20%) and to resilience (8 of the 11 resilience answers are voice), while typed answers carry almost all the technology/science hope (11 of 13); AI comes up three times, twice as a worry about its energy and water use.

5 answers garbled or unusable.

political-profile-views · page 70 · issue-importance

Election issues, in their own words

There are many topics being discussed in the U.S. today. In your own words, which issues matter most to you in the upcoming election ?

thematic codingbase: 125 answers46 voice / 79 typed

Shared codes, pilot 2 → pilot 3 (share of answers)

What matters most to me is the general cost of goods and services in our country right now and being able to afford necessities such as groceries and paying rent. voice
Affordability, ending current wars, and restoring sanity and checks and balances to government. We must root out corruption, prosecute those who have damaged the republic, and build a better working democracy for all Americans. So say I. typed
I'm so completely unplugged from political subjects. I don't even know what issues are in the upcoming election. voice
Basic human rights, such as abortion, LGBTQ rights, handling immigration and racism and the economy. Making things like gas, houses, and groceries affordable again is a major issue to me. typed

Economy / inflation / cost of living is the modal theme at 56 of 125 answers (45%, vs 41% in pilot 2), with groceries, gas, rent, tariffs and taxes as the recurring specifics. Leadership, division, integrity doubled to 18% (23) from 9%, driven by democracy and election-fairness framings (12 answers mention democracy, election cheating or fairness, or a president becoming a dictator); Civil rights / abortion / trans rights (15% vs 7%), Climate / energy (16% vs 10%) and Immigration (14% vs 10%) are also up, while War / foreign policy (13% vs 16%), Healthcare (12% vs 14%), Explicitly partisan (10%, unchanged), Housing / social security (6% vs 9%) and Crime / safety (3% vs 7%) are flat or lower. Disengaged / don't know fell to 10% (12) from 17%, but half of those (6) are garbled captures rather than stated disengagement. Twelve of the 13 partisan answers lean against Trump or Republicans (one is pro-Republican), two of them using an insulting epithet for the president that is not quoted, and one anti-immigration answer uses xenophobic framing. Voice answers (46 of 125) are longer and more multi-issue but account for 5 of the 6 garbled answers and 9 of the 12 Disengaged codes, whereas typed answers are mostly one- or two-word issue lists; Education (4 mentions) is added as a new code and AI (3 mentions) stays in Idiosyncratic.

6 answers garbled or unusable.

climate-who-cares · page 27 · climate-who-cares-open

Who cares about climate (gated: similarity 1–2)

When you think about someone who cares about climate change, what kind of person comes to mind ?

thematic codingbase: 99 answers40 voice / 59 typed

Shared codes, pilot 2 → pilot 3 (share of answers)

A responsible person that cares about the environment and nature. voice
I'm going to say left-wing, drives an electric car, is a science enthusiast. typed
Unfortunately for me, most people active in climate change activism are radicals who point out problems, but have zero solution or implementation of efforts. voice
The majority of the time, it’s someone that already does things differently than the average person… vegans.. extremely fit and energetic… well off financially typed

Environmentalist / steward is the modal theme at 29 of 99 answers (29%, vs 28% in pilot 2), usually described through behaviours such as recycling, composting, avoiding plastic, veganism or driving an electric car; together with Caring, kind, empathetic person (16, 16% vs 19%) the steward/caring cluster covers 41 answers (41%). Derogatory or hostile caricatures appear in 19 answers (19%, vs 23% in pilot 2; 23% when Extreme / worrier framings are included), ranging from 'tree hugger' and 'crazy hippie' to 'leftist loser', 'fascist liberal', 'easily fooled' and 'looking for a purpose in life', and political labels (liberal, Democrat, left-wing, politician) appear in 10 answers (10%, down from 19%). Two new codes were needed: 'Nobody comes to mind' (10, 10%; nine of the ten are typed, mostly a bare 'none' or 'no one') and 'A specific person' (5, 5%: a partner, a father, family and friends, Greta Thunberg and Dwayne Johnson); Scientists / professionals rose to 12% (12) from 4%, Non-answer to 11% (11) from 6% and Extreme / worrier framing to 7% from 4%, while Activist (4%), Denial-adjacent (3%), 'No particular type' (5%) and Worried parents (1%) are close to pilot 2. All 7 unusable answers (six garbled or off-topic captures and one complaint about the survey) are voice, i.e. 18% of the 40 voice answers versus none of the 59 typed; otherwise hostile (18% voice vs 20% typed) and steward (30% vs 29%) shares are similar across modes.

poster-wallbase: 274 completes163 cards seen by ≥1 participant

Most-loved, as a share of those shown the card: Marvel Universe 23%; Shrinking 23%; Wednesday 22%; Hijack 20%; Landman 20%. Auto-generated distributions for all 106 closed items with pilot-3 answers, in instrument order (page numbers refer to the 71-page fielded order): single-choice and Likert items as counts, matrices as row means, multi-selects as option shares, long numeric scales bucketed. 10

Data quality and analysis caveats

Ten things to hold onto before analyzing these rows.

  1. The field was open when this page was generated. Numbers run through Sep 13, 2026 5:57 PM ET; the 73 parked rows will partly convert, so completion and mid-survey abandonment will move. Regenerate before quoting final figures.
  2. Segment pilot 3 on total_pages = 71 and a capture time on or after Sep 12, never on created_at (session reuse). Ten Sep-11 rows on the same build are team checks (nine without a Forthright rid, one localhost) and are excluded here.
  3. Pilot 2 is recomputed with the same exclusions (302 arrivals / 143 completes). Its own tab reports 318 / 145 because 14 localhost ops-launch rows and 2 named team rows were still counted there; the pilot-1 figures (213 / 71) are unchanged.
  4. Landing clearance here means leaving page 0 (spoken pass, typed phrase, or any recorded fallback), so it is comparable across the three landings; the spoken-pass rate is no longer the landing completion rate. Typed entrants carry Botcheck_Voice.Passed = 0 and Botcheck_Voice.Fallback = typed_phrase; condition bot-rate analyses on it (ADR 0051).
  5. Three show walls write into one Shows key. Split cards by the per-wall sampling records (_posterwall_Shows_Network, _posterwall_Shows_Sports, _posterwall_Shows_Streamer), not by id prefix; the streamer record’s sample lists the 75 cards actually shown. 23 completes never saw the streamer wall (no streaming platform reported).
  6. Use active dwell, not wall-clock, for speed screening. 11 completes show under 8 minutes of active time on a 132-question instrument and should be reviewed; 12 exceed an hour (backgrounded tabs).
  7. Straight-lining is present but not extreme: 26 completes (9%) gave an identical answer to every row on three or more matrices; the flat matrices concentrate on Media.Message (71), Climate_Response.Efficacy (64) and M.Motive_Parasocial (51), where uniform agreement is also a plausible honest answer.
  8. Identity checks: 3 Forthright rids appear on two rows each (re-entries; de-duplicate on rid before analysis), 0 field rows lack a rid, 6 browsers report a non-English language and 5 report a non-US timezone (Europe/Paris 1, Europe/London 2, Europe/Berlin 1, UTC 1). The honeypot caught nobody.
  9. Reloads reset session-scoped telemetry (landing event log, blocked-tap counts); treat struggle counts as lower bounds. 10 rows logged client errors, all from browser extensions, none from the survey.
  10. Attempt transcripts and gate audio remain temporary pilot diagnostics with no automated purge; deletion after the pilot is still a manual step that has not happened.

Entertainment Lab · Wave 2 Audience Segmentation

Pilot 2 Readout

First field of the rotation-era instrument: mobile-eligible, telemetry-instrumented, 2-of-5 voice rotation. A living readout — data still accruing.

Generated Sep 08, 2026 15:18 UTC318 starters · 145 completesPublish w2-final-fielding-fr7b · source 8d2c3b17
OverviewFieldLanding telemetryRotationVoiceOpen-endsAll itemsCaveats
01

Overview

Pilot 2 is the first field on the 79-question rotation-era instrument (published Sep 1, 19:46 UTC, source 8d2c3b17): phones and tablets eligible for the first time, landing-page telemetry active, the gate’s audio retained, and the five ungated voice probes rotating 2-of-5. Data below runs through Sep 08, 2026 15:18 UTC and is still accruing toward the ~100-complete ask.

Field notes in one paragraph. Pilot 2 ran in two waves on evolving builds: a phone-heavy Sep-1 evening wave (phones ~72% of arrivals, 73% of them passing the spoken gate) and a desktop-heavy Sep-3 daytime wave that pulled the device mix to roughly half phone, half desktop — desktops passing the gate at just 41%. From Sep 3, 02:15 UTC the live build (source cdda1ef6) added classified gate-recovery fallbacks and a structured MFQ draw (ADR 0048), so pilot 2 itself spans regimes; 16 completes entered through the new fallbacks and carry Botcheck_Voice.Fallback with a failure classification. The 2-of-5 rotation drew within sampling noise of even, every shown open item was answered, and about half of open answers came by voice. The main quality caveat is measurement, not respondents: session reuse and reloads make created_at, capture-time durations and single-load telemetry unreliable for returning devices (pre-Sep-3 builds; the Sep-3 build persists telemetry across reloads). Details in section 08.

02

How the field went

Bovitz re-opened the tap about 35 minutes after the republish and released in waves; the survey converted steadily behind each wave.

traffic

Arrivals came in batches, ~50/hour at peak

Arrivals per hour (UTC), by first capture on the landing page.

trafficbase: all 318 starters

Traffic began at 20:21 UTC, ran in visible batch releases with dry gaps of 10–20 minutes between them, peaked around 23:00–00:00 UTC, and tapered after 01:00. 155 sessions remain parked mid-survey; some will resume and convert — the row store updates in place when they do.

funnel

318 starters &rarr; 177 past the gate &rarr; 145 completes

Where arrivals stood at generation time.

funnelbase: all 318 starters

Of 318 arrivals, 177 (56%) passed the spoken check and 145 have completed. 18 gate-passers were terminated by the Zanadu attention row (10% of gate-passers — a normal panel rate), and none by the honeypot.

devices

Phones carried the field

Arrivals, gate passage, and completion by device class (classified from the landing capability probe).

device splitbase: all 318 starters

Phones: 147 arrivals, 65% passed the gate, 50% completed. Desktops: 157 arrivals with 45% gate passage. The desktop shortfall is not fumbled permissions — see the landing analysis: most desktop gate deaths never tapped the microphone at all.

timing

Median completion 15.4 minutes

Completion time measured from landing capture to the completion save; active dwell sums the per-page timers.

durationsbase: 144 completes

Capture-to-complete overstates time for participants who background the tab (max 135m) and understates it for those who reload late (a reload rewrites the capture stamp — one apparent 0-minute complete). Active dwell is the analysis-grade measure; the two medians agree within half a minute.

03

Landing page: the full diagnostic picture

Pilot 1 could not tell a blocked microphone from an ignored one. The telemetry shipped for pilot 2 stamps every arrival with a capability probe and logs every tap, grant, denial and notice — so for the first time each of the 141 landing losses has an attributable cause.

capability probe

What arrivals brought to the page

Passive probe at page load: mic permission state, input devices, secure context. No permission prompt fires.

telemetrybase: 316 probed arrivals

288 of 316 arrivals (91%) had never been asked for their microphone — the gate is almost always the first ask. Only 5 arrived pre-denied. 16 arrivals reported no microphone hardware at all: automatic gate deaths that pilot 1 would have booked, unexplained, as screener terminations.

gate outcomes

Three ways to die at the gate, now countable

Every arrival ends the landing in one of three states.

mic gatebase: all 318 starters

The dominant loss is refusal to engage: 81 arrivals (25%) read the “say ‘I am human’” ask and left without one tap — concentrated on desktop. 60 tried and could not get through (permission blocks, transcription failures, no-mic hardware). Browser permission machinery itself was cooperative: 119 permission-state change events were recorded — typically the prompt-to-granted grant — and pre-denied browsers were nearly absent.

blocked taps

38 arrivals fought a blocked microphone

attempt_mic_blocked entries in the bot-check log — taps where the browser refused the mic stream. That covers both a participant tapping Don't-allow on the permission popup and a device- or browser-level block where no popup appears; the log records the refusal, not the reason. Logged per attempt since the Sep-1 fix.

telemetrybase: 38 arrivals with a blocked tap

Two distinct frictions separate cleanly in the log. Permission friction: 38 arrivals tapped and were refused — some declining the popup themselves, some facing a settings-level block (a post-refusal permission state of ‘denied’ marks the persistent blocks; ‘prompt’ usually marks a declined or dismissed popup). One entrant tapped 24 times before giving up — a pattern that fits a dead, hard-blocked button rather than 24 separate refusals. Transcription friction: 47 “couldn’t transcribe” notices — the mic granted, speech recorded, but STT failing to return the phrase; in the session timelines reviewed these cluster on phones, with participants retrying three to five times and some abandoning with a working microphone. That second group is the cheapest fixable loss at the gate.

Reloading the landing page resets the in-memory log, so blocked-tap counts undercount strugglers who reload; treat these as lower bounds.

retained audio

The gate now keeps its audio

Since this publish the spoken check uploads its recording to the private interview-audio bucket, like every other voice item.

audiobase: 195 arrivals with gate utterances

Attempt transcripts remain capped, temporary, metadata-only diagnostics; the response row still records only the pass/used booleans.

regime 3

Gate-recovery fallbacks (from Sep 3, 02:15 UTC)

The cdda1ef6 build lets a participant continue after repeated classified failures; Botcheck_Voice.Fallback records why.

gate changebase: 16 fallback completes

16 completes entered through a classified fallback — mic access failures, denied or ungranted permissions, timeouts, and repeated no-speech or phrase mismatches. These are exactly the willing-but-blocked and STT-friction losses the Sep-1 telemetry identified; the new build converts them into completes with an auditable flag instead of gate deaths. Funnel note: completes from Sep 3 onward therefore include participants whose Botcheck_Voice.Passed is 0.

04

The 2-of-5 voice rotation

Five ungated voice-first probes now rotate two per participant on a seeded draw recorded to _pm_questions_voice-open-rotation; the similarity-gated who-cares probe rides on top for those in [1,2].

draw balance

Draws balanced at arrival; every pair occurred

Times each item was shown, over completes with a draw record. Expected 40% each.

planned missingnessbase: 145 completes

Across all arrivals the five items drew 34–50% against the 40% expectation, and over completes each of the ten possible pairs occurred (11–21 times). An early trust-world overdraw (73% at n=11) regressed to 48% as n grew — verified twice by simulation over the production seed and id shape as sampling noise, not mechanism bias. Every draw is reconstructible from the row, so residual imbalance is weightable.

gated probe

Who-cares gate fired for 34% of completes

climate-who-cares-open shows only when Climate_Concerned.Similarity ∈ [1,2].

showIf gatebase: 145 completes

Participants drawn out of both trust items and gated out of who-cares saw exactly two open probes; the page-skip machinery — pinned by the instrument test suite — hid those pages whole; no empty-page anomaly has surfaced in the dwell records.

05

Voice against typing

With the forced gate upstream, 51% of open-ended answers arrived by voice — and voice answers ran about 2.2× longer than typed ones.

uptake

175 of 340 open answers came by voice

Voice share per shown item, completes only.

voice vs typedbase: 340 answers

Every shown item was answered by every completer — the fallback keyboard caught everyone who declined the mic. Voice share is statistically flat across items (46–59%); an early zero on IssueImp (last page) dissolved with n. Mean utterance ran 19s.

answer quality

Voice answers ~28 words; typed ~13

Mean answer length by input mode, all open items pooled.

qualitybase: 175 voice / 165 typed

The richness gap replicates pilot 1’s finding at scale. The cost side is real but modest: roughly one voice answer in ten is unusable as a transcript — a foreign-language STT pass, television crosstalk, or a mis-hear (“Cumo”) — versus about one in sixteen typed. Retained audio now makes the voice junk partially recoverable by human listening.

06

Open-ended answers, thematically coded

All 340 substantive open-ended answers were read and coded against per-item codebooks; answers can carry multiple codes. Chips mark voice or typed exemplars; one answer is characterized but not quoted. This is the full-corpus pass over all 329 substantive answers at the 141-complete mark (Sep 3). The Sep-3 daytime wave — desktop-heavy, fielded on the third build regime — reads more politically charged than the Sep-1 evening wave: explicitly partisan issue answers, more climate denial, and a re-politicized who-cares stereotype; the per-item notes call these out.

trust-messengers-open · page 34

TV-world trust: distrust first, entertainers second

“Who are some TV figures or celebrities that you trust to talk about the world — for example, the economy or politics?”

thematic codingbase: 60 answersmulti-coded
I don't trust any of them. Why would I want TV figures or celebrities talking about politics? A lot of them are just narcissistic and only care about themselves. voice
Not many people. I guess I like Stephen Colbert, Jon Stewart, and John Oliver. They may be comedians but they call the world for what it is and generally stand up for people who need help typed
I would have to say that I trust Marco Rubio, J.D. Vance… maybe Clint Eastwood when he was younger or John Wayne when he was alive. voice
None of them, people who are allowed to become celebrities in this world are mostly bought and paid for mouthpieces for the Bourgeoisie. voice

The modal answer is a refusal of the premise: 37% trust no TV figure on the world, often with articulate reasons (out of touch, bought, narcissistic). Trust that is granted goes first to entertainers and athletes as individuals (Steph Curry, Dolly Parton, Denzel Washington), then to comedian-anchors whose appeal is explicitly “they call it what it is.” Named answers span the political spectrum — Obama and Doechii next to Rubio, Vance, Charlie Kirk, Joel Osteen, and one vote of confidence in Donald Trump; the Sep-3 wave added Rogan, Gutfeld, Jim Cramer and a Mexican YouTuber, plus one answer of “Optimus Prime.”

trust-messengers-open · page 35

Climate trust snaps to scientists

“Who are some people you trust to talk about climate change? They don't have to be TV figures or celebrities — anyone counts.”

thematic codingbase: 51 answersmulti-coded
Mainly, I trust scientists and some sort of teachers that are in science or adjacent to it. voice
There is no individual that i trust regarding climate change, but if a group of scientists can agree than we should listen to them. typed
I would be comfortable talking about climate change with my significant other, my friends, my family, my pastor, pretty much anyone. voice
Grand Solar Minimum News, Dane Wigington, Extinction Rebellion XR UK typed

The contrast with the world question is the finding: distrust collapses from 40% to two respondents in thirty-seven, celebrities collapse from twelve namings to two (Katt Williams, Travis Scott), and scientists — generic or by field: geologists, meteorologists, ecologists, one respondent’s own lab advisor — hold 41% at the larger n. The strong second channel is personal: family, friends, a pastor, a spouse, grandchildren, a boss, a late mother (27%). One Sep-3 answer named Jesus; another was a verbatim PediaSure commercial the mic transcribed off a television. Bill Nye and Neil deGrasse Tyson are the only crossover figures named on both questions.

climate-solution-recall · page 43

Solutions recalled: individual acts first, corporations close behind

“In your opinion, what are some of the most effective ways to address climate change? Please list as many as you can think of.”

thematic codingbase: 58 answersmulti-coded
I think that big corporations are the ones that need to make the biggest change, but that people like myself can also participate in simple things like recycling, using public transportation… voice
Vote for legislators who actually care about climate change and will create laws… Also confronting the corporations and companies that affect climate change negatively and regulate their emissions. typed
stop using this generative ai, protecting forests, FINALLY switching to renewable energy sources typed
I feel like one of the most effective ways is addressing the billionaires and the corporations. You know what they say, things start at the top. voice

Unaided recall leads with the household repertoire — recycle, drive less, waste less (31%) — while a quarter of answers point upward at corporations, billionaires or legislators, several fusing both levels unprompted. Three respondents independently named AI data centers as an emissions driver, an emergent 2026 theme no roster would have offered. A fifth could not produce a solution at all, and denial grew with the Sep-3 wave to seven answers (12%) — from “climate change is a hoax” to a proposal to “get rid of all the green stuff.” A fourth respondent named AI data centers, this time proposing to force builders onto alternate energy.

climate-efficacy · page 55

Hope is concrete and local — where it exists

“What gives you hope when you think about humanity's efforts to mitigate, adapt and resolve climate change?”

thematic codingbase: 55 answersmulti-coded
It gives me hope when I see my friends and neighbors putting out their recycle bin every week instead of just throwing things away. voice
Humanity has overcome all kinds of adverse things in history, and they've always been able to come out on top. voice
What gives me hope is people with large platforms and influence spreading awareness on serious matters, so that their audience can take action and be inspired to help. typed
Actually, I'm not really hopeful right now about that. Several changes would have to be made, especially in our Congress… voice

Where hope exists it is strikingly concrete — neighbors’ recycling bins, cleaned waterways, communities working together — rather than technological or institutional. A fifth of answers report little or no hope, and the hostile tail (“this is a really stupid question”) is worth remembering when interpreting item nonresponse on hope-adjacent scales.

political-profile-views · page 78

Election issues: the economy, then everything else

“In your own words, which issues matter most to you in the upcoming election?”

thematic codingbase: 58 answersmulti-coded
Inflation, the economy, can't afford to live, can't afford to go on vacation. We're fighting from paycheck to paycheck and can't get our kids anything. No after-school activities, no sports. It's just too expensive. voice

Cost of living dominates unaided salience at 41%, with one answer compressing it to a sentence — quoted below. The Sep-3 wave introduced a code the Sep-1 wave barely needed: six answers whose core issue is defeating the other party, split between both parties. Immigration still divides into protection and enforcement framings; climate or energy surfaces unaided in six of fifty-eight answers (10%). A sixth of respondents are simply disengaged.

climate-who-cares · page 47 (gated)

Who cares about climate: stewards to some, caricatures to others

thematic codingbase: 47 answersmulti-coded
People who are empathetic, people who care about the Earth, people who care about others. voice
When I think about someone who cares about climate change, I think about the marine biologists that study the ocean and the meteorologists… they're the ones that alert the audience and the world. voice

Idiots typed

Recall the gate: these are respondents who feel least similar to climate-concerned people, yet 43% still describe a steward or a kind, caring person. The hostile share runs from one-word dismissals (“Psychos”, “a unserious person”) to one profanity- and slur-laden rant caricaturing EV-driving granola stereotypes (characterized here, not quoted). Political labeling — “a liberal”, “DEMOCRATS”, “woke” — tripled with the Sep-3 desktop wave to 19%, close to pilot 1’s all-desktop 20%: the politicized stereotype appears to travel with the panel wave and device mix rather than with time. The combined tab sets these codes against pilot 1’s.

08

Data quality and analysis caveats

Six things to hold onto before analyzing these rows.

  1. Date rows by metadata.embeddedData._capture_time, not created_at. A returning device reuses its stored session id and upserts into its old row; one pilot-2 complete sits on an Aug-28 created_at.
  2. A reload rewrites session-scoped telemetry. The landing event log, blocked-tap counts and the capture stamp reflect the latest page load; treat struggle counts as lower bounds and prefer per-page dwell sums for duration (one apparent 0-minute complete is consistent with a late reload, not a bot).
  3. The two sub-4-minute wall-clock completes are not speeders. Their capture stamps were reset by late reloads; per-page dwell shows 9.8 and 37.5 minutes of active time, zero fully-flat matrices (baseline ~6% among normal completes), passed attention checks, and substantive voice answers. Use dwell sums, never capture-to-complete, for speed screening — by active time no pilot-2 complete finished under 4 minutes.
  4. All pilot-2 traffic post-dates the bot-check double-log fix, so _botcheck_voice_attempts counts are clean here; pilot-1-era counts are not comparable.
  5. Rotation draws are recorded per row (_pm_questions_voice-open-rotation); any shown-set imbalance is reconstructible and weightable.
  6. Attempt transcripts remain a temporary pilot diagnostic with no automated purge; deletion after the pilot is a manual step that has not yet happened.
  7. Pilot 2 spans build regimes. From Sep 3, 02:15 UTC (source cdda1ef6): gate-recovery fallbacks (completes may carry Botcheck_Voice.Passed = 0 plus a Botcheck_Voice.Fallback classification), a structured MFQ draw (ADR 0048 — 1 per foundation + 3 extras, superseding the pure 9-of-36 draw), and reload-persistent telemetry. Split gate and MFQ analyses on the capture timestamp.
  8. One copy-paste respondent: the same irrelevant string (“with the larva being consumed…”) pasted into three different open items — flagged for exclusion from qual analyses; a second row answered climate trust with a transcribed television commercial.

Entertainment Lab · Wave 2 Audience Segmentation

Pilots 1 + 2, Combined

Cross-pilot traffic comparison, the shared who-cares construct, pooling rules, and pooled distributions for every closed item.

Generated Sep 08, 2026 15:18 UTC531 starters · 216 completes pooledPilot 1: Aug 28–31 · Pilot 2: Sep 1–2
OverviewTrafficWho caresPooling rulesPooled items
01

Two pilots, one table

Pilot 1 (Aug 28–31, 74-question build, desktop-only) and pilot 2 (Sep 1–3, 79-question rotation build, all devices, third-regime build from Sep 3) share survey_id audseg-w2-final and one response table. This tab compares their traffic and pools what is poolable. The Aug-26 Connect timing pilot, transitional rows and team tests are excluded throughout.

02

Traffic, side by side

Same panel, same entry links, same gate — different devices and a longer instrument. Nearly every funnel difference traces to the device mix.

funnel

The funnel, pilot against pilot

Percent of starters reaching each stage.

comparisonbases: 213 vs 318 starters

Gate passage nearly doubled, 40% → 56%, and the never-tapped share halved, 56% → 25%. Completion rose from a third to a half of starters despite five more questions — pilot 2 is still converting, so its final rate will edge higher. Attention terminations ran at similar, normal rates in both.

device

Pilot 1 was a desktop-only funnel; pilot 2 is a phone funnel

Device mix of starters.

comparisoncapability probe (p2) / UA (p1)

Pilot 1’s desktop-only gate turned away every mobile entrant as a screener termination — the origin of the “20% incidence” misread. Freed, the panel’s natural mix is 46% phone; and phones out-perform pilot-1 desktops at every stage: 65% gate passage vs 40%, 50% completion vs 33%. Pilot 2’s own desktops still pass at only 45% — the gate is largely a desktop tax.

throughput

Completes per fielded hour

Completions per hour of active fielding (p1 over ~2 evening sessions; p2 over ~5 hours).

comparison

Pilot 2 filled roughly twice as fast per active fielding hour (both hour counts are rough estimates of active-release time) — mobile eligibility widened the pipe more than the added questions narrowed it. Median duration rose about two minutes on five extra questions; the rotation kept three voice pages out of each participant’s path.

attribution

What pilot 1 couldn't see

Share of landing losses with an attributable cause.

telemetrythe diagnostic delta

Pilot 1 recorded nothing between arrival and the gate verdict: 128 losses, zero explained — the readout could only infer. Pilot 2 explains all 141: 81 never engaged, 60 engaged and failed, with permission states, notices and blocked-tap counts under each. The instrumented never-tapped rate (25%) also supports reading pilot 1’s dominant loss as refusal-to-engage rather than technical failure — an inference, not a measurement, since pilot 1 lacked the probe; it rests on pilot 2’s arrivals (including its desktops) showing a near-universal ‘prompt’ state and its losses concentrating among those who never tapped.

03

Who cares about climate — the cross-pilot construct

The one open probe fielded identically in both pilots, to the same gated population (similarity 1–2), coded with one codebook. Pilot 1: 25 substantive answers, desktop typers and speakers; pilot 2: 26, phone-heavy.

thematic comparison

The stereotype is stable; its politics soften

Share of answers carrying each code (multi-coded).

thematic codingbases: 25 vs 47 answers

The core image replicates almost exactly: a steward-environmentalist described warmly by about half of pilot 1 (52%) and 43% of pilot 2 once code overlap is de-duplicated, a hostile caricature from about a quarter — remarkable stability for n≈25 samples a few days apart on different devices. The one clear mover is political labeling (“a liberal,” “DEMOCRATS,” “woke”): 20% in all-desktop pilot 1, 9% in pilot 2’s phone-heavy first wave, back to ~19% once the desktop-heavy Sep-3 wave arrived — suggesting the politicized stereotype tracks panel wave and device mix, not time. A “no particular type — anyone” code still appears only in pilot 2.

voice uptake

The gate-as-investment finding replicates

Voice share on who-cares among those shown it.

voicethe pilot-1 headline, retested

Pilot 1’s striking observational result — 56% voice uptake downstream of a forced spoken gate, versus 18% with no gate in the Connect probe — repeats on phones within noise. But the causal interpretation is now contested: a randomized landing-page experiment on Connect (Sep 3, three arms, n≈40/arm) found voice uptake statistically flat whether the gate was present or not (58% ungated vs 59–69% gated), while the gate cost a third of arrivals. The original 18% benchmark likely reflected other design differences, not the absence of a gate. The gate’s funnel cost is causal; its uptake benefit is not established.

04

What pools, what doesn't

Rules of the road for joint analysis of the 155 pooled completes.

  • Pools cleanly: every closed item fielded in both builds (66 shared response keys), the who-cares probe (adjacency to climate-personal-normative was preserved), attention/honeypot outcomes, and completion behavior — with a pilot indicator and device class as covariates.
  • Pools with care: durations (different instrument lengths; use active dwell), voice uptake (device mix shifted), and anything downstream of the five rotated items (pilot 2 shows each to ~40% by design — weight by the recorded draw).
  • Does not pool: the trust pair (reworded to standalone forms for pilot 2; pilot 1 never fielded them), solution-recall / hope / issue-importance (pilot 2 only), landing telemetry (pilot 2 only), and _botcheck_voice_attempts counts (pre-fix rows double-log).
  • Regime marker: segment pilots on total_pages (43 vs 45) or the presence of _pm_questions_voice-open-rotation; never on created_at. Within pilot 2, split gate and MFQ analyses at Sep 3, 02:15 UTC — the cdda1ef6 build changed the gate (recovery fallbacks) and the MFQ draw (ADR 0048).

Entertainment Lab · Wave 2 pilots 1+2 · Generated Sep 08, 2026 15:18 UTC · Data: Supabase audseg_survey_responses
Entertainment Lab · Audience segmentation · Wave 2

Pilot survey readout: every question, charted

Bovitz fielded the Wave 2 instrument to its Forthright panel in a soft launch beginning the evening of Aug. 28. Of the 210 panelists who started the survey, 70 completed all 43 pages, a 33% completion rate. This report examines every question in the instrument.

Field window: Aug. 28–29, 2026Completes: 70 of 210 startsMedian completion: 16 minutesSource: audseg_survey_responses
Field diagnosisLanding page and bot checksMedia habitsShow wallsViewing motives and audience demandPsychological scales and religionClimate beliefs and social normsEfficacy, willingness, policy and politics
Overview

How the field went

210

middle half took 11 to 22 minutes

no completer tripped the timer

The one big loss was the landing page: 128 of 210 starters (61%) never got past the bot checks, almost all at the microphone step. Whoever got in, finished.

Diagnosis

Why incidence read 20%

The panel paused collection over a 20% incidence rate, 243 screener terminations and 30% dropout. All three trace to two design gates, not to data problems.

243
mobile clicks bounced
booked by the panel as screener terminations
96%
of true dropouts stopped at the mic
120 never tried it, 8 failed
7
attention-check exits
9% of entrants — normal
15%
clicks became completes
about 1 in 6

The 243 “screener terminations” were the fielded build’s desktop-only gate bouncing the panel’s ordinary mobile traffic — 54% of clicks — under the screening exit code. The dropout was the mic check: 128 of 133 true dropouts died on the landing page. Inside the survey, 70 of 82 finished (85%) with no speeder flags. Net yield: 15% of clicks became completes.

The desktop gate — Prolific-era boilerplate, never an ADR’d decision — was removed Aug. 31 (commit 18bfa51a); phones and tablets are eligible in the next batch. The mic check stays, so mobile respondents will meet it on mobile permission prompts: quotas belong on completes, not invites, and the telemetry below should ship before fielding resumes.

Section

Landing page and bot checks

The opening block pairs a welcome page with three bot defenses: a Turnstile widget, a spoken confirmation and a hidden honeypot item.

What the landing page can and cannot record

Every signal below lands in the response row’s metadata. A session row is created by the first save, which fires when Turnstile verifies — nothing earlier is observable first-party.

SignalFires whenWhat it answers
Row + Turnstile passServer verifies the token (edge function)Real-browser check; creates the session record
Voice utterance telemetryEach completed recordingSTT mode, duration, transcription latency, auto-stop reason — content-free
Voice used / passed flagsFirst utterance / fuzzy phrase matchWhether the spoken check was attempted and cleared
Honeypot responseOnly if the hidden item is selectedScripted-form automation
Diagnostics snapshotEvery saveBrowser, OS, screen, touch, network, timezone, language
Client error logUncaught JS errors (last 20)Crashes and script failures
Page dwell (timing_*)On leaving the pageActive seconds per page — completers spent a median of 30s on the landing page
Mic button tapNever recordedCannot count who tried
Browser permission outcomeDenial is a screen message only; nothing persistsCannot split “never clicked” from “clicked, mic blocked”
Turnstile failure or abandonmentA failed check never creates a rowPre-Turnstile exits are invisible
Device-gate redirectFires before any saveMobile bounces countable only from panel dispositions
Dwell for landing-page abandonersTiming writes on page exit within the appZero of the 120 stuck sessions carry it

The landing page by the numbers

210
desktop starters created a row
243 mobile clicks were redirected before any row
210 of 210
passed Turnstile

90 (43%)
