82 of 90
passed the spoken check
91% of attempts; 8 failed

Everyone who created a row passed Turnstile; nobody tripped the honeypot. The page’s one real filter was the microphone: 128 of 210 starters stopped there (120 never tapped it, 8 failed), and everyone else went on to answer questions.

Landing-page telemetry for pilot 2 — shipped

Six additions were proposed, all metadata-only. Items 1–4 and 6 shipped Aug. 31 (commit 3c21c934) and are live in the fielding build; item 5 became moot when the device gate was removed, and device class is captured in the arrival snapshot instead. Verified end to end: an arrival with a pre-blocked microphone now records permissionState denied before any tap, and a failed tap writes the full mic_tap → mic_not_granted → permission-state chain.

  1. Persist mic-tap events. Record each tap on the mic button with a timestamp and save immediately. Answers: how many of the silent 57% ever tried.
  2. Persist the permission outcome. The recorder already distinguishes blocked (NotAllowedError), no device (NotFoundError) and success; write that result instead of only showing a toast. Answers: refusal vs. browser-blocked vs. broken hardware.
  3. Snapshot mic capability on page load. Permissions-API state (granted / denied / prompt), audio-input device count, secure-context and API-support flags, saved with the first row. Answers: how many arrive with the mic already blocked before any tap.
  4. Create the row at page load, not at Turnstile pass. First save on mount, plus an explicit turnstile_failed event. Answers: pre-Turnstile abandonment, currently invisible.
  5. Beacon the device-gate redirect. One fire-and-forget event with disposition device before the mobile redirect, and map the exit to the engine’s device terminal reason so the panel stops booking it as screening. Answers: first-party mobile bounce count.
  6. Flush dwell on tab close. Send timing and the latest diagnostics via sendBeacon on pagehide. Answers: how long abandoners stared at the mic ask before leaving.
1 intro-consent

Landing page frames 20-minute survey and two bot checks

Information page

The landing page welcomes panelists, describes a roughly 20-minute survey covering background, media habits and views on environmental and social topics, and presents the two bot checks as safeguards against AI bots contaminating the data.

2 intro-consent

All 210 starters pass the Turnstile check

“Check 1 of 2: please complete the box below.”

Bot checkbase: all 210 starters

Every panelist who started the survey cleared the Turnstile widget, with 210 of 210 passing for a 100% pass rate.

3 intro-consent

Voice check draws 90 attempts from 210 starters

“Check 2 of 2: tap the mic button and say: “ I am human .””

Voice or textbase: all 210 starters

Ninety of the 210 starters, or 43%, used the microphone prompt asking them to say "I am human." Of those who tried, 82 passed, a 91% pass rate.

Because the check is required, the gap between 210 starters and 90 attempts marks the survey's largest apparent abandonment point and may warrant a nonvoice fallback.

4 intro-consent

Hidden honeypot item goes untouched by all starters

“Confirmation”

Single choicebase: all 210 starters

None of the 210 starters selected the hidden honeypot item, and the trap recorded zero hits across the soft launch.

A clean honeypot screens out only unsophisticated bots and does not rule out more capable automation.

Section

Media habits

5 mh-genre

Drama rates highest among genres, sci-fi/fantasy lowest

“Please indicate how much content you watch from each of the following genres :”

Matrixbase: 5–19 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

Drama scores highest at 3.5 on the zero-to-four viewing scale; all eight respondents asked said they watch quite a bit or a great deal. Sci-fi/fantasy scores lowest at 0.82, with 10 of the 11 asked saying not at all or a little. Comedy posts the highest mean among genres with at least 15 responses, at 2.88 among the 17 asked.

Each respondent rated three randomly assigned genres of 16, so item bases run from five to 19 and means are unstable.

6 mh-networks

NBC tops past-30-day broadcast viewing at 66%

“In the past 30 days , have you watched TV shows on any of the following networks ? Tap each one you've watched.”

Poster wallbase: completers shown each title (sampled walls vary by design)

NBC leads broadcast reach at 66% (46 of 70), followed by ABC at 64% and CBS at 57%. Univision trails at 3%. The median respondent tapped four of the 11 networks shown.

7 mh-networks-detailed

Viewers report regular or occasional watching across networks

“How often do you watch TV shows on the following networks ?”

Matrixbase: up to 23 completers per rowconditional

Among respondents shown networks they had watched, both Univision viewers asked said they watch regularly, the top mean at 3.0 on the zero-to-three scale. CBS leads the larger bases at 2.71, with 15 of the 21 asked saying regularly, and BET scores lowest at 2.25, with three of the eight asked saying regularly.

The question displays only networks selected earlier, so item bases run from two to 23 and most sit under 20.

8 mh-streaming

Amazon Prime Video and Netflix lead streaming frequency

“How often do you watch TV shows on the following streaming platforms (or, through Premium Channels) ?”

Matrixbase: up to 70 completers per row

Amazon Prime Video scores highest at 1.94 on the zero-to-three scale, with 47% of the 70 completers watching regularly, followed by Netflix at 1.71 with 44% regularly. Starz is the lowest-scoring real platform at 0.34, with 79% saying never. All 70 respondents said they never watch Zanadu+, the decoy platform included as a data-quality check.

9 mh-consumption

Introduction page opens the consumption block

Information page

An information page introduces the media and entertainment habits block before the hours-per-day items; it collects no data.

10 mh-consumption

Shared stem sets up hours-per-day entries

Information page

A shared stem instructs respondents to enter whole hours per day, from zero to 20, for each viewing activity that follows; it collects no data.

11 mh-consumption

Median weekday TV viewing is five hours

“Watching TV shows and movies — typical weekday (Mon–Fri)”

Text entrybase: 70 of 70 completers

All 70 completers answered, reporting a median of five hours and a mean of 7.8 hours watching TV shows and movies on a typical weekday. Entries range from zero to the 20-hour maximum.

The mean exceeds the median by nearly three hours, pointing to a tail of very high entries worth screening before full launch.

12 mh-consumption

Weekend TV viewing also runs five hours at median

“Watching TV shows and movies — typical weekend day (Sat–Sun)”

Text entrybase: 70 of 70 completers

Respondents report a median of five hours and a mean of 6.31 hours of TV shows and movies on a typical weekend day, with entries from zero to 20; all 70 completers answered.

The weekend mean runs below the weekday mean, an atypical pattern that may reflect the same high weekday entries flagged above.

13 mh-consumption

Social video fills two weekday hours at median

“Watching videos on social media (e.g., Instagram, TikTok, Facebook) — typical weekday (Mon–Fri)”

Text entrybase: 35 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

Of the 35 respondents rotated into the social media item, the median respondent reported two hours per weekday watching videos on platforms such as Instagram and TikTok. The mean is 3.51 hours, with a high of 13.

The rotation shows each respondent either the social media or the video-platform items, halving the base to 35.

14 mh-consumption

Weekend social video viewing holds at two hours

“Watching videos on social media (e.g., Instagram, TikTok, Facebook) — typical weekend day (Sat–Sun)”

Text entrybase: 35 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

The 35 respondents asked report a median of two hours and a mean of 3.17 hours watching social media videos on a typical weekend day, with a high of 12.

The rotated design halves the base to 35 respondents.

15 mh-consumption

Video-sharing platforms draw one weekday hour at median

“Watching videos on video-sharing platforms (e.g., YouTube, Vimeo) — typical weekday (Mon–Fri)”

Text entrybase: 35 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

Of the 35 respondents rotated into the video-platform item, the median respondent reported one hour per weekday watching video-sharing platforms such as YouTube. The mean is 1.97 hours, and one entry reached the 20-hour maximum.

The rotated design halves the base to 35, and the 20-hour entry inflates the mean.

16 mh-consumption

Weekend video-platform viewing stays near one hour

“Watching videos on video-sharing platforms (e.g., YouTube, Vimeo) — typical weekend day (Sat–Sun)”

Text entrybase: 35 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

The 35 respondents asked report a median of one hour and a mean of 2.09 hours on video-sharing platforms on a typical weekend day, with one entry at the 20-hour maximum.

The rotated design halves the base to 35 respondents.

17 mh-social-platforms

Facebook leads past-30-day platform use at 79%

“Which of these online / social media platforms have you used in the past 30 days ? Tap each one.”

Poster wallbase: completers shown each title (sampled walls vary by design)

Facebook tops platform use at 79% (55 of 70), followed by Instagram at 50% and TikTok and X at 33% each. No respondent selected Truth Social, and the median respondent used two of the seven platforms listed.

Section

Show walls

18 shows-intro

Practice card teaches the tap-to-rate poster mechanic

Practice page

The page introduces the TV-show section and presents a practice poster card: one tap indicates the respondent watched most episodes of the latest season and a second tap marks a loved show. The wall pages that follow add that a third tap clears the selection.

19 shows

'The Simpsons' and 'Bob's Burgers' lead broadcast-cable selections

“First, here are shows from broadcast and cable networks , one section at a time. Tap once — you watched most episodes of its latest season. Tap again — a show you loved. A third tap clears it.”

Poster wallbase: completers shown each title (sampled walls vary by design)

Across the full show grid, respondents saw 305 of the 370 titles in the pool, and 280 of those drew at least one selection. The median respondent marked 14 shows as watched or loved (mean 18.9). Among broadcast and cable titles, 'The Simpsons' and 'Bob's Burgers' tie for the lead at 18 selections each, from the 42 panelists shown 'The Simpsons' (43%) and the 59 shown 'Bob's Burgers' (31%). NHL (16 of 52, 31%) and 'Scrubs' (16 of 39, 41%) follow at 16 apiece. Four of the 70 completers marked no show on this wall's grid.

Grid-level figures span both walls because responses share one Shows variable, and per-title bases range from six to 70 respondents by design, so single-title percentages are volatile.

20 shows-streamer

'Fallout' and 'Landman' pace the streaming show wall

“Next are shows from the streaming services you said you access , one section at a time. Tap once — you watched most episodes of its latest season. Tap again — a show you loved. A third tap clears it.”

Poster wallbase: completers shown each title (sampled walls vary by design)conditional

This conditional wall showed 166 titles drawn from services each respondent reported having, and respondents marked a median of 4.5 streaming titles (mean 8.1); 17 of the 70 completers marked none. 'Fallout' leads on volume with 19 selections among the 46 panelists shown it (41%), while 'Landman' posts the highest hit rate among titles shown to at least 20 respondents, at 13 of the 25 shown (52%). 'Hijack' rated higher on a small base, drawing six selections of the 11 shown.

Per-title bases run from six to 53 respondents because display was conditioned on service access, so title-level rates carry wide margins.

Section

Viewing motives and audience demand

21 mm-engage

Fan content tops show engagement; posting ranks last

“For your favorite shows , how often do you...”

Matrixbase: 27–42 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

On a five-point scale from never to all the time, engaging with fan-created content such as blogs and podcasts scored highest (mean 2.45, n=42) and posting about shows on one's own social media accounts scored lowest (mean 1.74, n=27). All four items averaged below the scale midpoint of sometimes.

Each respondent saw two of the four items, so bases ranged from 27 to 42 rather than the full 70.

22 mm-viewing-motivation

Escape ranks first among viewing motives, social talk last

“When you watch TV shows or movies, how important is each of the following reasons for you?”

Matrixbase: 31–38 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

Rated on a 0-4 importance scale, escaping daily life and unwinding ranked highest (mean 2.63, n=38), followed by relaxing with something familiar and comforting (mean 2.54, n=37). Having something to talk about with friends, family or online ranked lowest by a wide margin (mean 1.29, n=31).

Planned missingness showed each respondent two of the four items, so bases ranged from 31 to 38.

23 mm-parasocial-short

Viewers most admire favorite characters' problem-solving

“In general, for the TV shows and movies I most enjoy watching :”

Matrixbase: up to 70 completers per row

All 70 completers rated four parasocial statements on a five-point agreement scale. Wishing to handle problems as well as a favorite character scored highest (mean 3.29, with 34 of 70 neutral), while following trends and ideas from the actor who plays a favorite character scored lowest (mean 2.66).

24 md-messaging-actions

Intro page opens personal beliefs and choices section

Information page

An informational page introduces the personal beliefs and choices section, telling respondents the survey will ask about the impact of movies and TV shows on their beliefs and choices.

25 md-messaging-actions

Discussing show issues common; petition signing absent

“Setting aside news and documentaries... Have you taken any of the following actions based on something you learned from a movie or TV show?”

Matrixbase: 19–34 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

Asked whether they had taken actions based on something learned from a movie or TV show, 65% (22 of 34) said they had discussed an issue with someone, the highest rate of the eight actions, while none of the 27 asked had signed a petition, the lowest. Three of the 19 asked said they had changed a habit.

Each respondent saw three of the eight items, so bases ranged from 19 to 34, and the item with a base under 20 is reported as a raw count.

26 md-audience-demand-general

71% say Hollywood should show climate-friendly actions on-screen

“We are interested in your opinion about whether Hollywood should play a role in combating climate change. Previous research has found that, by showing characters on-screen taking positive actions, Hollywood contributed to: Reduced rates of smoking Reduced rat…”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Asked whether studios and streaming platforms should include climate-friendly actions on-screen to help address climate change, 50 of the 70 completers (71%) said yes and 20 (29%) said no.

27 md-audience-demand-behaviors

Slider page introduces on-screen climate behavior battery

Information page

An instruction page introduces a battery of oppose-support sliders asking whether Hollywood should show more of five climate-related behaviors on-screen.

28 md-audience-demand-behaviors

Green energy depictions draw strongest on-screen support

“Renewable / Green Energy Show more "green energy" on screen (e.g. roof-top solar panels, solar farms, wind farms, etc.) Show more character or scenes involving "green jobs" (e.g. clean energy sector)”

Sliderbase: 24 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

On a slider from minus 100 (oppose) to 100 (support), showing more green energy such as rooftop solar, wind farms and green jobs drew a median of 78.5 and a mean of 41.3 among the 24 asked. Seventeen respondents landed on the support side and seven on the oppose side.

Planned missingness cut the base to 24, so estimates are imprecise.

29 md-audience-demand-behaviors

Green transport scenes also lean toward support

“Low-Emissions / Green Transport Show more electric cars, trucks, and other vehicles Show more scenes involving public transit (e.g., buses, trains, and subways) Show more scenes with low or zero carbon transport (e.g. bikes, scooters, ebikes)”

Sliderbase: 19 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

Showing more electric vehicles, public transit and low- or zero-carbon transport drew a median of 60 and a mean of 36.3 on the minus 100-to-100 oppose-support slider among the 19 asked.

With a base under 20, results are directional only.

30 md-audience-demand-behaviors

Climate consequence scenes get moderate support from small base

“Climate Depictions Show more scenes highlighting the consequences of climate change”

Sliderbase: 12 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

Showing more scenes highlighting the consequences of climate change drew a median of 45.5 and a mean of 30.7 on the minus 100-to-100 oppose-support slider among the 12 asked.

The base of 12 is too small for reliable inference; the mean-median gap reflects a few strong opposers.

31 md-audience-demand-behaviors

Respondents split nearly evenly on plant-based diet depictions

“Reducing meat / Eating a more plant-based diet Show more plant-based meals at restaurants or homes Include more vegetarian or vegan characters”

Sliderbase: 70 of 70 completers

All 70 completers rated showing more plant-based meals and vegetarian or vegan characters on the minus 100-to-100 oppose-support slider. The median was minus 1.5 and the mean minus 2.8, with 36 respondents on the oppose side and 34 on the support side, the only behavior tested that did not lean toward support.

32 md-audience-demand-behaviors

Climate activism scenes earn modest support

“Getting Engaged Show more characters engaging in climate activism (e.g. community organizing, protests, advocacy) Show more characters talking about climate change (e.g. their fears, hopes, etc.)”

Sliderbase: 15 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

Showing more characters engaging in climate activism or talking about climate change drew a median of 31 and a mean of 15.9 on the minus 100-to-100 oppose-support slider among the 15 asked, the weakest support among the behaviors that leaned positive.

With a base under 20, results are directional only.

Section

Psychological scales and religion

33 need-for-cognition

Respondents embrace problem-solving but split on avoiding hard thinking

“Please indicate how much you agree with the following statements:”

Matrixbase: up to 70 completers per row

All 70 completers rated three need-for-cognition statements on a five-point agreement scale. The highest-scoring item, "I really enjoy a task that involves coming up with new solutions to problems," averaged 3.67, with 64% agreeing or strongly agreeing. The lowest, preferring tasks that require little thought over mentally challenging ones, averaged 2.9, with 29 of 70 disagreeing and 23 agreeing.

34 trait-reactance

Frustration over restricted decisions tops trait reactance items

“Please indicate how much you agree with the following statements:”

Matrixbase: 43–50 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

Planned missingness showed each respondent two of three reactance items, putting item bases at 43 to 50. The highest-scoring item, frustration at being unable to make free and independent decisions, averaged 3.77 on the five-point scale, with 65% of the 43 asked agreeing or strongly agreeing. The lowest, doing exactly what is prohibited, averaged 2.74, with 26% of the 47 asked agreeing or strongly agreeing.

35 mfq

Care item rates highest, income-equality item lowest

“For each of the statements below, please indicate how well each statement describes you or your opinions.”

Matrixbase: 10–29 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

Each respondent saw nine of 36 Moral Foundations items rated 0-4 on how well each statement describes them, leaving item bases of 10 to 29. The top item, "Caring for people who have suffered is an important virtue," averaged 3.22, with nine of the 18 asked choosing "extremely well." The lowest, getting upset when some people have much more money than others, averaged 1.05, with nine of the 20 asked choosing "not at all."

Per-item bases as small as 10 make individual item means unstable; foundation-level patterns are more informative than single items.

36 religiosity

Most respondents say religion holds little importance

“How important is religion in your life?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Asked how important religion is in their lives, 36% of the 70 completers said not at all important and 21% said slightly important, while 33% said very or extremely important. The mean was 1.54 on the 0-4 scale and the median respondent landed at slightly important.

37 religiosity

Nearly half never attend religious services

“Aside from weddings and funerals, how often do you attend religious services?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Aside from weddings and funerals, 46% of the 70 completers said they never attend religious services and another 16% said seldom. At the other end, 17% reported attending once a week or more, including one respondent attending more than once a week.

38 religiosity

Protestants lead affiliations as more than a third claim none

“What is your present religion , if any?”

Drop-downbase: 70 of 70 completers

Protestants are the largest group at 26 of 70 respondents (37%), followed by Catholics at 10 (14%). Respondents identifying as atheist, agnostic or nothing in particular total 25 (36%). Jewish, Buddhist, Hindu, Mormon, Orthodox and "something else" responses account for the remaining nine.

39 religiosity

About a third of Christians identify as born-again

“Would you describe yourself as a born-again or evangelical Christian ?”

Single choicebase: 40 completers shown this questionconditional

Among the 40 respondents shown this conditional item, 14 (35%) described themselves as born-again or evangelical Christians and 26 (65%) did not.

The item displays only to respondents with a qualifying religious affiliation, so the 40-person base is not the full completes sample.

40 religiosity

Majority welcomes faith leaders discussing environmental care

“How would you feel if your community's pastor/priest/faith leader talked about the importance of caring for the environment in their sermons, preaching or other church-related activities and conversations?”

Single choicebase: 45 completers shown this questionconditional

Among the 45 respondents shown this conditional item, 56% said they would feel positive if their faith leader talked about caring for the environment, including 14 who said very positive. Another 29% were neutral and 16% negative, for a mean of 0.69 on the scale from minus 2 to plus 2.

The conditional 45-person base limits precision; the display rule should be verified before full launch.

Section

Climate beliefs and social norms

41 environmental-ypccc

Slim majority rates global warming personally important

“How important is the issue of global warming to you personally ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

A slim majority of the 70 completes, 54%, said the issue of global warming is extremely or very important to them personally, led by 30% who chose extremely important. Another 30% said it is not too or not at all important.

42 environmental-ypccc

Two-thirds worry at least somewhat about global warming

“How worried are you about global warming?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Four in 10 respondents (40%) said they are very worried about global warming and 26% said they are somewhat worried, a combined 66%. One in five (20%) is not at all worried.

43 environmental-ypccc

One-third expects no personal harm from global warming

“How much do you think global warming will harm you personally ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

One-third of respondents (33%) said global warming will not harm them personally at all, while 16% expect a great deal of harm and 24% a moderate amount. Two of the 70 said they don't know.

44 environmental-ypccc

Half see great harm to future generations

“How much do you think global warming will harm future generations of people?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

About half of respondents (51%) said global warming will harm future generations a great deal, more than three times the 16% who expect that much harm personally. Another 21% foresee moderate harm to future generations and 17% expect none at all.

45 climate-temporal-proximity

Nearly four in 10 say climate impact has arrived

“When do you expect climate change to start having a meaningful impact on your daily life ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

The most common answer, from 37% of respondents, was that climate change already has a meaningful impact on their daily life, and 67% expect that impact now or within roughly the next nine years. At the other pole, 21% said it won't have an impact on them.

46 climate-lived-impact

One-third reports no lived climate change effects

“To what extent have you personally experienced the effects of climate change?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

One-third of respondents (33%) said they have not personally experienced the effects of climate change at all, while 23% report a moderate amount, 14% quite a bit and 9% a great deal. The mean is 1.44 on a 0-4 scale.

47 climate-lived-impact

Heat leads past-year extreme weather reports

“In the past year , has the area where you live experienced any of the following? Select all that apply.”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Heat was the most commonly reported event of the past year, cited by 46% of respondents, followed by wildfire at 30% and drought at 29%. Storm (26%) and flood (21%) trail, and 27% selected none.

All selections landed on shortened labels while the questionnaire's full option wordings show zero counts, a value-coding mismatch to resolve before full launch.

48 environmental-identity

Personal responsibility to reduce climate change runs moderate

“To what extent do you feel a personal responsibility to try to reduce climate change ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

The most common answer was "somewhat," chosen by 34% of respondents, and the mean is 2.96 on a 1-5 scale. A combined 31% feel quite a bit or a great deal of personal responsibility to reduce climate change, while 23% feel none at all.

49 climate-personal-normative

Nearly eight in 10 endorse climate action as right

“Do you think that people should take action to address climate change because it is the right thing to do ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Most respondents, 55 of 70 or 79%, said people should take action to address climate change because it is the right thing to do. The remaining 21% said no.

50 climate-who-cares

Respondents see climate-concerned people as somewhat similar

“How similar are the people who care about climate change to you ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Respondents rated people who care about climate change a mean 2.94 on a 1-5 similarity scale, with "somewhat like me" the most common answer at 30%. A combined 34% said such people are a lot or very much like them, while 17% said "not at all like me."

51 climate-who-cares

Open-ended item collects images of climate-concerned people

“When you think about someone who cares about climate change, what kind of person comes to mind ?”

Voice or textbase: 25 completers shown this questionconditional

The 25 respondents shown this open-ended follow-up described the kind of person who comes to mind as someone who cares about climate change. Responses ran a median of 15 words and a mean of 28.3, with the longest at 175 words.

Conditional display limited the base to 25 of the 70 completes.

52 climate-empirical-expectations

Median guess: Four of 10 valued others act

“Imagine 10 people whose opinion matters to you. If you had to guess, how many of them do you think currently take actions to address climate change ?”

People pickerbase: 70 of 70 completers

Asked to imagine 10 people whose opinion matters to them, the median respondent guessed four currently take actions to address climate change. The mean guess is 4.06 of 10 (n=70).

53 climate-dynamic-norms

Most expect valued others' climate action to hold steady

“Imagine 10 people whose opinion matters to you. Do you think in the coming years, more or fewer of them will take action to address climate change because it is the right thing to do?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Nearly half of respondents (47%) expect about the same number of valued others to take climate action in the coming years, while 41% expect more and 11% expect fewer. The mean is 0.39 on a scale running from minus 3 to 3.

54 climate-normative-expectations

Perceived approval of climate action outpaces perceived action

“Imagine 10 people whose opinion matters to you. If you had to guess, how many of them think that other people should take actions to address climate change because it is the right thing to do ?”

People pickerbase: 70 of 70 completers

The median respondent guessed 5.5 of 10 people whose opinion matters to them think others should take climate action because it is the right thing to do, compared with a median of four guessed to currently act. The mean is 5.34 (n=70).

55 climate-talk

Most discuss global warming occasionally at most

“How often do you discuss global warming with your family and friends?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

More than four in 10 respondents (44%) said they rarely or never discuss global warming with family and friends, while 30% do so occasionally and 26% often or very often. The mean is 1.69 on a 0-4 scale.

56 climate-talk

Avoiding climate talk outscores finding it tense

“Please indicate how much you agree with the following statements:”

Matrixbase: 23–24 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

Of the three agree-disagree statements, "I tend to avoid bringing up climate change in conversation" scores highest at a mean 2.74 of 5, and "the conversation usually gets tense or unpleasant" scores lowest at 2.30. Respondents split on whether people talk about climate change too much, with 10 of 24 agreeing and 10 disagreeing.

Planned missingness showed each respondent one of the three statements, leaving item bases of 23 to 24.

Section

Efficacy, willingness, policy and politics

57 climate-efficacy

Personal climate efficacy runs low

“How confident are you in your ability to personally make a difference on climate change?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Nearly half of respondents (47%) said they are not at all or only slightly confident they can personally make a difference on climate change, compared with 20% who are very or extremely confident. The item averaged 1.47 on a scale from 0 (not at all confident) to 4 (extremely confident) among all 70 completes.

58 climate-efficacy

Collective action inspires more confidence than individual

“How confident are you that people working together have the ability to make a difference on climate change?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Respondents expressed more faith in people working together, with a mean of 2.01 on the same 0-4 scale. About 36% said they are very or extremely confident collective action can make a difference on climate change, compared with 20% for personal action, and 16% said they are not at all confident.

59 climate-responsibility-attribution

Government and corporations bear most climate responsibility

“How much responsibility does each of the following have for addressing climate change ?”

Matrixbase: 33–38 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

On a 1-5 scale from none at all to a great deal, respondents assigned the most responsibility for addressing climate change to the government (mean 3.73) and corporations (3.71), with the top 1% close behind (3.65). People like themselves scored lowest at 3.23.

Each respondent rated two of the four randomly shown items, so item bases range from 33 to 38.

60 other-key-beliefs

Respondents back lifestyle change, reject techno-optimism

“Please indicate how much you agree with the following statements:”

Matrixbase: 32–37 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

The statement that individual lifestyles must change to protect the world for future generations drew the highest agreement (mean 3.61 on a 1-5 scale), narrowly ahead of reforming government for the same goal (3.59). The claim that new technologies will solve climate change without major changes to how we live scored lowest (2.12), with no respondent strongly agreeing.

Each respondent saw two of the four randomly shown statements, so item bases range from 32 to 37.

61 climate-willingness-intention

Slim majority expects to act within a year

“Please indicate how likely it is that you will take some action to address climate change in the next 12 months ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

A slim majority (53%) said it is at least somewhat likely they will take some action to address climate change in the next 12 months, while 29% said it is unlikely, including 19% who chose extremely unlikely. The mean was 0.36 on a scale from minus 3 (extremely unlikely) to 3 (extremely likely).

62 climate-coalition-building

Most open to climate compromise across political divides

“Imagine people who disagree with you on most important social, political and cultural issues. How willing are you to work with them to find compromise solutions for addressing climate change?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Two in five respondents (40%) said they are very or extremely willing to work with people who disagree with them on most issues to find compromise climate solutions, and 13% said they are not at all willing. The item averaged 2.04 on a 0-4 scale.

63 climate-willingness-seek-info

Email sign-up interest splits nearly even

“Please indicate if you would be willing to receive more information via e-mail on how you can take action to address climate change.”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

A narrow majority (53%, or 37 of 70) said they would be willing to receive more information by email on how to take action on climate change; 47% said no.

64 climate-policy-single-issue

Most could still vote for a climate-opposed candidate

“Imagine a political party or candidate that agrees with you on the vast majority of issues . However, they oppose robust action on climate change . Could you ever vote for them?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Asked about a hypothetical candidate who agrees with them on most issues but opposes robust climate action, 57% of respondents said they could still vote for that candidate, while 43% said they could not.

65 climate-income-contribution

Most balk at contributing 1% of income

“Would you be willing to contribute 1% of your household income every month to fight global warming? This would mean that you would contribute $1 for every $100 of this income.”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

A majority (61%) said they would not be willing to contribute 1% of household income every month to fight global warming; 39% said they would.

66 environmental-actions

Preamble introduces environmental actions section

Information page

An informational page tells respondents the next section asks about their actions and views related to the environment; it collects no data.

67 environmental-actions

One in four donates to environmental nonprofits

“In the past 12 months, have you donated money to any environmental nonprofit (for example, World Wildlife Fund, Sierra Club, or The Nature Conservancy)?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Seventeen of 70 respondents (24%) said they donated money to an environmental nonprofit such as World Wildlife Fund, Sierra Club or The Nature Conservancy in the past 12 months; 76% said no.

68 envprof-publicaction-page

One in 10 reports environmental protest participation

“In the last 12 months, have you participated in any demonstrations, marches, rallies, or other events in support of an environmental cause ?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

One in 10 respondents (seven of 70) reported taking part in a demonstration, march, rally or other event in support of an environmental cause in the last 12 months.

69 policy-general-support

Clean-energy incentives outpoll drilling policies

“How much do you support or oppose the following policies?”

Slider matrixbase: 21–30 completers per row (random subset by design)planned missingness

On a slider from minus 100 (oppose) to 100 (support), tax rebates for energy-efficient vehicles or solar panels drew the strongest support (mean 50.6, median 77), followed by generating renewable energy on public land (mean 49.4, median 64). Drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge scored lowest (mean minus 28.6, median minus 34), and expanded offshore drilling was also net negative (mean minus 14.2).

Each respondent rated three of the eight policies, leaving item bases of 21 to 30 that make individual policy estimates imprecise.

70 political-profile-views

Sample tilts slightly left of center

“In political matters, people talk of "the left" and "the right." How would you place your views on this scale, generally speaking?”

Sliderbase: 70 of 70 completers

On a 0 (left) to 10 (right) scale, the median respondent sat at the midpoint of 5 and the mean was 4.63. The midpoint was the most common answer (18 of 70), while 17 respondents placed themselves at 0 or 1 and seven at 10.

71 political-profile-views

Harris leads Trump in recalled 2024 vote

“In the 2024 presidential election , did you vote? If so, for whom?”

Single choicebase: 70 of 70 completers

Half of respondents (35 of 70) said they voted for Harris in the 2024 presidential election and 40% said they voted for Trump. The remaining seven voted for another candidate, did not vote, were ineligible or declined to answer.

72 political-profile-views

Biden leads recalled 2020 vote among subset

“In the 2020 presidential election , did you vote? If so, for whom?”

Single choicebase: 40 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

Of the 40 panelists shown the item, 22 (55%) said they voted for Biden in 2020 and 11 (28%) for Trump; the other seven voted for someone else, did not vote or were ineligible.

The item displays to a random subset under planned missingness, so the 40-person base limits precision.

73 political-profile-views

Democrats edge Republicans in 2022 midterm recall

“In the 2022 midterm elections , which best describes how you voted?”

Single choicebase: 30 completers randomly assigned this questionplanned missingness

Among the 30 respondents asked, 13 (43%) said they voted for Democrats in the 2022 midterms and 11 (37%) for Republicans, while four did not vote, one split the ballot and one was ineligible.

The 30-person base under planned missingness makes these shares rough estimates.

74 demo-survey-basics

All completes supply valid ZIP codes

“What is your 5 digit ZIP code?”

Text entrybase: 70 of 70 completers

All 70 respondents who completed the survey entered a valid five-digit ZIP code, indicating clean capture on the text-entry item.

About this report

Internal readout for Rare. Base: the 70 completes from the Aug. 28–29 soft launch; bot-check figures use all 210 starters. Bases vary by design (planned missingness, conditional display, sampled walls) — small-base items report counts, not percentages. Matrix rows sort by mean; poster walls show titles seen by at least eight respondents. AP number style throughout.
